title: The wind as incense
hook: tradition sets this hymn at Puri, where Nanak saw a temple aarti and pointed to the one the universe performs

segments.voice: Yesterday, aarti, and your line: the sky is the platter. Did you catch one ordinary thing and see it on the tray? Today, the story Sikhs tell about where this hymn was first sung. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

The east coast of India, the Bay of Bengal. A town called Puri, home to the great temple of Jagannath, Lord of the World. Pilgrims still walk there. The janamsakhis, the old collections of stories about Guru Nanak's life, say he came here on his long journeys, with his companion Mardana, the musician who played the rabab. Evening came, and the temple's aarti began: lamps on golden trays, incense, bells, crowds. And the stories say that Guru Nanak stood quietly and didn't join in.
screen: `PURI, ON THE BAY OF BENGAL.` → `NANAK AND MARDANA ARRIVE.` → `THE EVENING AARTI BEGINS.`

segments.voice: In one telling, someone notices the visitor standing apart and asks why he isn't taking part in the aarti. In reply, Guru Nanak asks Mardana to play, and he sings: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. The fragrant breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, the forests are the flowers. What a wonderful aarti this is. The aarti, he says, has been going on the whole time. It's just bigger than the temple. Hold this story as tradition. The hymn itself doesn't name Puri, and the janamsakhis were written down after Guru Nanak's lifetime and don't always agree in detail. What the hymn does say is in its later verses, and they turn the picture inside out. In paraphrase: You have thousands of eyes, and yet no eye. Thousands of forms, and yet not one form. Thousands of feet, yet no foot; thousands of noses, yet no nose. And then: within everything is a light, and that light is You. By that light, all are lit. So the wind isn't only incense. The wind, the stars, the forests, the people at the temple, the people standing apart: all of them are lit by the same light. The story, as Sikhs tell it, isn't about scorning anybody's lamps. It shows Guru Nanak widening the circle until the whole world is inside the offering, the priests, the pilgrims and the two travelers too.
screen: `WHY AREN'T YOU JOINING IN?` · `THE AARTI HAS BEEN GOING ON ALL ALONG.` · `THOUSANDS OF EYES, YET NO EYE.` · `ONE LIGHT, AND ALL ARE LIT.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE WORLD OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: smell the evening air. Open a window, or step outside, or simply breathe in slowly where you are. What's in it? Cut grass, rain, exhaust, someone's cooking, the dryness of an air conditioner. Whatever it is, let it be the incense in the hymn, carried to you on the wind. Breathe it in, and breathe out slowly. Then once more, a little slower. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
The wind as incense. In Sohila's third hymn, the breeze carries the fragrance and the wind waves the fan: the whole world performing the aarti.
Your line: the whole world offering. Today, when you feel a breeze or catch a smell on the air, let it remind you that the aarti, in the hymn's picture, never stops. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly in Kirtan Sohila and sing it in gurdwaras as the Aarti; the story of Guru Nanak at Puri is often told alongside it, especially at gurdwara evening programs.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pavan, wind or breeze; in the hymn, the wind waves the fan for the universe's aarti.

trapdoor: what you thought: the wind as incense is a nice line about nature.
what it means: in the hymn's picture, the breeze and the wind are part of the aarti creation performs, lit by the one light in all.
what a scholar hears: the Puri setting comes from janamsakhi tradition, not the text; the hymn's later lines (sahas tav nain) describe the One as having countless forms and none.

notes: Puri story told as tradition (janamsakhi); details vary between janamsakhis. Confirm the version (Nanak asked why he did not join, Mardana plays, he sings the hymn) is the common one.
Later verses paraphrased ('thousands of eyes, and yet no eye; thousands of forms, and yet not one form'; 'within everything is a light, and that light is You; by that light all are lit'). Confirm.
Tone toward the temple aarti: written to avoid scorn and to present the story as widening the circle; confirm a Keeper is comfortable.
Gurmukhi ਪਵਨ (the hymn has the form pavan/pavanu); confirm.
